request: Should a 60-year-old with high cholesterol take statins? Walk through the expected years of life #interactive

spec.title: Statins at sixty: how much life?

details.value_statin: Folded back: $0.10 \times 16 + 0.90 \times 24 = 23.2$ years. The numbers are rounded illustrations for a 60-year-old with a ten-year risk of about 15 in 100; real gains depend on her own risk and how far the statin lowers her cholesterol.
details.payoff_n_event: An average over everyone who has a heart attack or stroke: some die of it, others live on with a shorter life expectancy. Illustrative.

sources.title: Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol: a meta-analysis of data from 170,000 participants in 26 randomised trials
sources.finding: Each 1 mmol/L lower LDL: about a fifth fewer events

sources.title: N-of-1 Trial of a Statin, Placebo, or No Treatment to Assess Side Effects
sources.finding: 90% of symptoms also came on placebo

commands.speak: Should a sixty-year-old with high cholesterol take a statin every day? It comes down to one question: how much longer will it let her live?

ask.question: On average, how many extra months of life does a statin give her? Click your guess on the line.
ask.right: Close. Your guess was {g}; the answer is about five months.
ask.wrong: Your guess was {g}; the answer is about five months. Most people guess years — hold on to that.

commands.speak: About five months, for a pill every day for decades. To see where that comes from, lay out what can happen.
A decision tree: the square is her choice, and each circle is chance taking over.
Without a statin, say fifteen in a hundred people like her have a heart attack or stroke within ten years.
The other eighty-five don't.
Life left from sixty: about twenty-four years with no event, sixteen on average after one, because some die of it and others live shorter lives.
A statin lowers cholesterol. A big pooled analysis of the trials found each step down cuts these events by about a fifth; for her, fifteen in a hundred becomes ten.
The ending years don't change: the statin only moves people between the branches.
Now weigh each ending by its chance. With a statin: point one times sixteen, plus point nine times twenty-four, is twenty-three point two years.

ask.question: Your turn: weigh the no-statin branch. How many years can she expect?

commands.speak: Twenty-three point two against twenty-two point eight: the statin wins by four tenths of a year — those five months.
But no one actually lives an extra five months. So who gains?

ask.question: Picture 100 people like her taking a statin for ten years. How many are spared a heart attack or stroke they would otherwise have had?
ask.right: Yes: you said {h}, and it is {h.true} — fifteen events become ten.
ask.wrong: You said {h}; it is {h.true}. Fifteen events become ten, so five are spared.

commands.speak: Ten still have one, statin or not.
And eighty-five never would have: for them the pill changes nothing.
The whole gain sits with these five. Each gets back about eight years: twenty-four instead of sixteen.
Five people times eight years is forty years of life…
…shared out over a hundred people: four tenths of a year each. Five months.
So the five months are an average nobody lives. What she is really offered is a one-in-twenty chance of about eight more years.
And it scales with her risk. Double it to thirty in a hundred, and the statin spares ten, and the average gain doubles too.
Back to her fifteen in a hundred.
What does she give up? A pill a day, and for some, aching muscles.
Yet in a 2020 trial, people who had quit statins over side effects took statin, dummy pill or nothing, month by month, without knowing which: ninety percent of the symptoms came with the dummy too.

So should she? England's guidelines offer a statin from a ten-year risk of ten in a hundred. The tree can't make her choice; it shows her the bet: a daily pill for a one-in-twenty chance at eight more years.

quiz.question: Her friend's ten-year risk is only five in a hundred. Cut by the same third, about how many of 100 like him does a statin spare?
quiz.right: About two: a third off five in a hundred is under two, so the same pill buys far less for someone at lower risk.
quiz.wrong: The statin cuts the risk by a third — a third of what?
